commands.name: ps
commands.summary: Display information about currently running processes.
cautions: Command lines shown by `ps aux` may contain passwords or tokens — and so do other users’ processes on shared hosts.
commands.explanation: ps takes a snapshot of processes. `ps aux` shows all processes for all users (BSD format). Columns include PID, %CPU, %MEM, and COMMAND. Combine with grep to find specific processes. For live views use top or htop.

flags.desc: User-oriented format: show USER, CPU%, MEM%
Include processes without a controlling terminal
Sort output (e.g. --sort=-%cpu for highest CPU first)

examples.desc: Find nginx worker processes and their PIDs
Show all processes as a parent-child tree

commands.pro_tip: Use `pgrep -la nginx` instead of `ps aux | grep nginx` — cleaner output that won't include the grep process itself.

commands.name: kill
commands.summary: Send a signal to a process — commonly used to terminate processes.
commands.risk_reason: SIGKILL (-9) immediately terminates without cleanup — can corrupt data.
cautions: `kill -9` gives the process no chance to clean up — send SIGTERM first and wait.
Verify the PID (`ps -p <pid> -o pid,user,cmd`) — PIDs get reused.
`kill -9 -1` / `kill -- -1` signals every process you can signal.
commands.explanation: kill sends signals to processes by PID. Default is SIGTERM (15) which requests graceful shutdown. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught and forces immediate termination — use as last resort. SIGHUP (1) typically reloads service config.

flags.desc: Force kill immediately — no cleanup, potential data loss
List all available signal names and numbers

examples.desc: Gracefully terminate process 1234 (gives it time to clean up)
Force-kill process by name when SIGTERM failed
Send SIGHUP to nginx to reload configuration without restart

safer.why: Confirm what you are about to kill.
Ask the process to stop cleanly first.

commands.pro_tip: Always try SIGTERM first, wait 5s, then SIGKILL. Jumping to -9 can corrupt databases and leave stale lock files behind.

commands.name: systemctl
commands.summary: Control the systemd init system and service manager.
commands.risk_reason: Starting, stopping, or disabling services directly affects system availability.
cautions: Stopping or disabling the wrong unit (sshd, networking, firewalld) can lock you out of a remote host.
`restart` drops connections; use `reload` where supported.
After editing unit files run `systemctl daemon-reload`, then check `systemctl status` and `journalctl -u <unit>`.
commands.explanation: systemctl manages service lifecycle (start/stop/restart/reload), enables services to start at boot, and queries status with recent logs. Always verify service status after restart in automated scripts.

examples.desc: Check nginx service status, PID, and recent log lines

examples.cmd: systemctl restart nginx && systemctl is-active nginx
examples.desc: Restart nginx and confirm it's running
Enable Docker at boot AND start it immediately

commands.pro_tip: Use `systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed` to see all failed services — great for post-reboot health checks.

commands.name: journalctl
commands.summary: Query and display systemd journal logs.
cautions: Logs may contain secrets and personal data; `--vacuum-size/--vacuum-time` permanently deletes old journals.
commands.explanation: journalctl is the primary tool for accessing systemd's structured binary journal. It supports filtering by unit, time range, priority, and boot. Unlike tail on flat log files, it understands log metadata and allows complex structured queries.

flags.desc: Show logs from current boot (-1 for previous)
Output format: json, json-pretty, short, verbose

examples.desc: Show errors from current boot only
Logs in a specific time window

commands.pro_tip: Use `journalctl -b -1 -p err` to review errors from the previous boot after a crash — far faster than reconstructing the timeline from multiple log files.

commands.name: lsof
commands.summary: List open files and network connections by processes.
cautions: Without filters lsof scans every process and file and can take minutes on busy hosts; use -p, -i or +D carefully (+D recurses).
commands.explanation: lsof (list open files) shows every file, socket, pipe, and device currently opened by processes. On Linux, everything is a file — so lsof reveals TCP connections, listening ports, deleted-but-open files, and which process holds a lock.

flags.desc: Show network connections (optionally filter by port)
List all open files in a directory

examples.desc: Show all files opened by PID 1234
Show files opened by www-data user
Find files deleted but still held open (disk space recovery)

commands.pro_tip: When `df` shows disk full but you can't find the files, run `lsof | grep deleted` — processes holding deleted files keep them consuming space until the process dies.

commands.name: crontab
commands.summary: View, edit, or manage per-user cron schedules for recurring jobs.
commands.risk_reason: Misconfigured jobs run commands automatically — potentially destructively.
cautions: `crontab -r` deletes ALL jobs without asking — and sits right next to -e on the keyboard.
Cron has a minimal environment (PATH, HOME); use absolute paths and redirect output.
Overlapping runs pile up — wrap jobs in `flock -n`.
commands.explanation: crontab manages scheduled jobs. The five time fields are: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day (1-31), month (1-12), weekday (0-7). `*` means any, `,` for lists, `-` for ranges, `/` for intervals. Always use full paths in cron commands.

examples.desc: Weekly report every Friday at 11:30 PM with full logging

commands.pro_tip: Use https://crontab.guru to visually verify cron expressions before deploying them.

commands.name: top
commands.summary: Real-time dynamic view of system processes, CPU, and memory usage.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only by default; kill commands inside top carry risk.
commands.explanation: top provides a live display sorted by CPU usage. Press M to sort by memory, k to kill a process, q to quit. -b runs batch mode for scripting.

flags.desc: Show processes for a specific user

examples.desc: Capture a single top snapshot for logging
Monitor only web server user processes

commands.pro_tip: Install `htop` — same as top but with color, mouse support, and a much cleaner UI: `sudo apt install htop`

commands.name: uptime
commands.summary: Show how long the system has been running and load averages.
commands.explanation: uptime displays current time, system uptime, number of logged-in users, and load averages for 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Load average represents the number of processes in runnable or uninterruptible state — should generally stay below CPU core count.

examples.desc: Show uptime in pretty format (e.g., 'up 2 days, 3 hours')

commands.pro_tip: Compare load average to your CPU count: `nproc` tells you cores. Load of 4.0 is fine on a 8-core box but critical on a 2-core one.

commands.name: hostnamectl
commands.summary: Query and set the system hostname, OS info, and machine identity.
commands.risk_reason: Changing hostname can affect network identity and break service configs that rely on it.
cautions: Changing the hostname can break software that stores it (monitoring, certificates, clustering, Kubernetes node names).
commands.explanation: hostnamectl manages three hostname types: static (persistent, stored in /etc/hostname), transient (runtime, overridden by DHCP), and pretty (human-readable display name). Running without arguments shows OS, kernel, hardware, and virtualization info — useful for inventory scripting.

flags.desc: Set the static system hostname persistently

examples.desc: Display full system identity: hostname, OS, kernel, arch, virtualization type
Permanently rename the system to prod-web-01
Set a human-friendly pretty hostname that can include spaces

commands.pro_tip: After setting a new hostname, update /etc/hosts to map 127.0.1.1 to the new name — tools that do reverse DNS lookups will otherwise hang.

commands.name: vmstat
commands.summary: Report virtual memory, CPU, and I/O statistics.
commands.explanation: vmstat provides a snapshot or continuous stream of system resource statistics: processes, memory, swap, block I/O, and CPU time. Ideal for diagnosing high CPU wait (wa column) indicating I/O bottlenecks, or high swap usage.

examples.desc: Calculate average CPU idle over time

commands.pro_tip: Watch the 'wa' (I/O wait) column in `vmstat 1` — consistently above 10-15% indicates disk is the bottleneck, not CPU. This is often misread as a CPU problem.

commands.name: iostat
commands.summary: Report CPU and disk I/O statistics.
commands.explanation: iostat (from sysstat package) reports CPU utilization and per-device disk I/O metrics including throughput (MB/s), IOPS, and await (average I/O wait time in ms). The -x flag provides extended per-device statistics essential for storage performance analysis.

examples.desc: Extended disk stats, every second, 5 samples

commands.pro_tip: In `iostat -x` output, focus on `await` (avg I/O wait ms) and `%util` (device saturation). `await` > 20ms or `%util` > 80% signals a storage bottleneck.

commands.name: free
commands.summary: Display total, used, and available system memory.
commands.explanation: free shows physical memory and swap usage. The 'available' column (not 'free') is what matters — it includes reclaimable cache and is what the kernel reports as usable for new processes. Buffers and cache are not 'wasted' memory.

examples.desc: Show memory usage in human-readable format

commands.pro_tip: The 'available' column is the only one that matters for capacity planning — ignore 'free'. Linux aggressively uses RAM for cache; that's normal and good.

commands.name: uname
commands.summary: Print system information including kernel version and architecture.
commands.explanation: uname displays kernel and system information. Commonly used to verify the kernel version before patching, check CPU architecture for binary compatibility, and in scripts that need to adapt behavior per OS or architecture.

examples.desc: Kernel version only (e.g., for module compatibility)

commands.pro_tip: In CI/CD scripts, use `uname -m` to detect architecture and pull the correct binary (amd64 vs arm64) — critical for multi-arch Docker image builds.

commands.name: lscpu
commands.summary: Display CPU architecture and topology information.
commands.explanation: lscpu reads CPU details from /proc/cpuinfo and sysfs, displaying architecture, byte order, cores, threads, NUMA topology, caches, and CPU flags. Essential for capacity planning, performance tuning, and understanding NUMA effects.

examples.desc: Check physical vs logical CPU counts
Extract CPU count in JSON pipeline

commands.pro_tip: Check 'NUMA node(s)' in lscpu output — applications unaware of NUMA topology can experience severe performance degradation on multi-socket servers.

commands.name: nproc
commands.summary: Print the number of available processing units.
commands.explanation: nproc prints the number of CPUs available to the current process (respecting CPU affinity and cgroups). Simpler than parsing lscpu. Useful for setting parallel job counts in scripts and Makefiles.

flags.desc: Print total number of processors, not just available

examples.desc: Number of CPUs available to current process
Total CPU count on the system

commands.pro_tip: Use `$(nproc)` in Dockerfiles for parallel builds: `RUN make -j$(nproc)` — builds in containers respects the container's CPU quota, not the host's full count.

commands.name: dmesg
commands.summary: Print or control the kernel ring buffer messages.
cautions: Kernel logs can reveal addresses and hardware details; on some systems reading them requires root or kernel.dmesg_restrict=0.
commands.explanation: dmesg displays kernel messages from the ring buffer — hardware detection, driver errors, disk issues, OOM killer events, and network events. The -T flag adds human-readable timestamps. Essential for diagnosing hardware failures, OOM events, and kernel panics.

flags.desc: Filter by level (err, warn, info, etc.)
Follow kernel messages in real time

examples.desc: Follow kernel log in real time

commands.pro_tip: After any unexplained process death, run `dmesg -T | grep -i killed` to check if the OOM killer was responsible — a common cause misdiagnosed as application bugs.

commands.name: sysctl
commands.summary: Read and write kernel parameters at runtime.
commands.risk_reason: Can destabilize the system or change security posture.
cautions: Runtime changes affect the whole host immediately and are lost on reboot unless persisted in /etc/sysctl.d/.
Wrong values (rp_filter, ip_forward, tcp tuning, vm.overcommit, kernel.panic) can break networking or crash services.
Record the old value first (sysctl -n <key>) so you can roll back.
commands.explanation: sysctl reads and modifies kernel parameters in /proc/sys/ at runtime. Changes are immediate but not persistent unless written to /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/. Used for tuning network stack, enabling IP forwarding, configuring VM behavior, and hardening.

flags.desc: Print only the value, not the name

examples.desc: Check if IP forwarding is enabled

safer.why: Note the current value before changing it.
Reload from config files to undo runtime experiments.

commands.pro_tip: For K8s nodes, always verify: `sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` and `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`. Missing these causes pod networking failures that are hard to trace.

commands.name: ulimit
commands.summary: Get and set resource limits for the current shell and child processes.
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect limits can starve processes or hide resource issues.
cautions: Limits set in a shell apply to that shell and its children only; persistent limits live in /etc/security/limits.d/ or systemd LimitNOFILE=.
`unlimited` removes protection against runaway processes.
commands.explanation: ulimit controls resource limits (open files, processes, stack size, core dumps) for the shell and its children. Limits come in two types: soft (current limit, can be raised by user) and hard (maximum ceiling, only root can raise). Critical for high-connection services.

examples.desc: Increase open file limit for this session
Check limits of a running process

commands.pro_tip: High-traffic services (nginx, node) need `nofile` set to 65536+ in /etc/security/limits.conf or systemd unit (LimitNOFILE=65536). Default of 1024 causes 'too many open files' at load.

commands.name: timedatectl
commands.summary: Query and configure system time, date, and timezone.
commands.risk_reason: Changing time can affect logs and scheduled jobs.
cautions: `set-time`/`set-ntp false` changes the system clock behaviour — time jumps break TLS, Kerberos, databases and log correlation.
commands.explanation: timedatectl is the systemd tool for managing system time. Shows current time, hardware clock, NTP sync status, and timezone. Used to set timezone for servers and verify NTP is active — critical for distributed systems and log correlation.

examples.desc: Show current time, timezone, and NTP status

commands.pro_tip: Always verify `NTP synchronized: yes` on new servers before deploying distributed applications — unsynchronized clocks cause mysterious TLS errors and log correlation failures.

commands.name: date
commands.summary: Display or set the system date and time; format timestamps.
commands.risk_reason: Setting time requires root; display is read-only.
cautions: `date -s` changes the system clock — it can break TLS, Kerberos, cron, logs and replication; use NTP/chrony instead.
commands.explanation: date displays the current date/time in configurable formats, or sets the system clock. Heavily used in scripts for generating timestamps, log filenames, and date arithmetic. The -d flag parses arbitrary date expressions.

examples.desc: Yesterday's date for log rotation scripts

commands.pro_tip: Use `date +%s` and arithmetic for measuring script execution time: `start=$(date +%s); ... ; echo $(($(date +%s)-start))s elapsed`

commands.name: watch
commands.summary: Repeatedly execute a command at intervals and display output.
commands.risk_reason: Runs commands repeatedly; avoid watch on write operations.
cautions: `watch` re-runs the command every interval — with kubectl, aws or API calls this can hammer the target or hit rate limits.
Do not watch destructive commands.
commands.explanation: watch runs a command every N seconds (default 2) and displays its output full-screen, highlighting changes. Perfect for monitoring dynamic state like pod counts, resource usage, or deployment rollouts without writing a custom loop.

examples.desc: Watch disk usage with change highlighting

commands.pro_tip: Use `watch -d` during rolling deployments to instantly spot when pod statuses change — the highlighting makes it obvious without having to scan all rows manually.

commands.name: nohup
commands.summary: Run a command immune to hangup signals (SSH disconnects).
commands.risk_reason: Processes continue after logout; remember to manage them.
cautions: Output goes to nohup.out in the current directory (can grow without limit) — redirect it explicitly.
commands.explanation: nohup runs a command that won't be killed when the terminal session ends (SIGHUP is ignored). Output goes to nohup.out by default. A quick alternative to tmux/screen for one-off long-running commands.

examples.desc: Run script in background, immune to hangup
Get PID of last backgrounded process

commands.pro_tip: Always redirect both stdout and stderr with `> out.log 2>&1` when using nohup — otherwise output goes to nohup.out in whatever directory you ran it from.

commands.name: fuser
commands.summary: Identify processes using files or sockets.
commands.risk_reason: With -k flag, can send signals to processes.
commands.explanation: fuser identifies which processes are using specified files, directories, or network sockets. Simpler than lsof for the specific question 'what is using this file/port?' Returns PIDs which can be targeted directly.

flags.desc: Verbose output including username and access type
All processes accessing the mount point

examples.desc: Verbose: show who has log file open
Find all processes accessing a mounted volume

commands.pro_tip: Before `umount` fails with 'device is busy', run `fuser -mv /mountpoint` to find exactly which process is holding the mount — saves the 'why can't I unmount this' frustration.

commands.name: logger
commands.summary: Send messages to the system log (syslog/journald).
commands.risk_reason: Writes to system log; flooding can fill log storage.
cautions: Do not log secrets — syslog is readable by many users and often shipped to central systems.
commands.explanation: logger writes messages to the system journal or syslog. Used in scripts to emit structured log entries that appear in journalctl alongside system logs — crucial for script audit trails and integration with centralized logging.

examples.cmd: logger -t deploy 'Deployment v1.2.3 started by ec2-user'

commands.pro_tip: Add `logger -t $(basename $0) "Starting: $0 $*"` to the top of every admin script — creates an automatic audit trail in journald for all script executions.

commands.name: sar
commands.summary: Collect and report system activity statistics over time.
commands.explanation: sar (System Activity Reporter) collects and reports CPU, memory, network, and disk statistics. Unlike vmstat/iostat which show current state, sar records historical data (when sadc daemon runs) enabling you to analyze what happened during an incident hours ago.

flags.desc: Read from a saved data file

examples.desc: Review CPU history from a saved report

commands.pro_tip: Enable sysstat's cron job (`/etc/cron.d/sysstat`) so sar continuously records history. After an incident, use `sar -u -f /var/log/sysstat/saNN` to replay what CPU/memory did during the event.

commands.name: at
commands.summary: Schedule a one-time command to run at a specified time.
commands.risk_reason: Schedules future execution; verify time zone and system time.
commands.explanation: at schedules commands for one-time execution at a specific future time, unlike crontab which recurs. Jobs are queued in /var/spool/at and run even if the user logs out. The atq command lists pending jobs; atrm removes them.
commands.pro_tip: Use `at` for maintenance tasks that should run exactly once (e.g., applying a configuration change at a specific time). Unlike cron, there's no risk of it accidentally running repeatedly.

commands.name: rsyslog
commands.summary: Configure and manage the rsyslog system logging daemon.
commands.risk_reason: Misconfiguration can stop system logging entirely.
cautions: A syntax error in rsyslog.conf can stop logging entirely — validate with `rsyslogd -N1`.
Forwarding logs over UDP can lose messages; use TCP/RELP with disk-assisted queues.
Rotate and cap local log files so /var does not fill up.
commands.explanation: rsyslog is the high-performance system logging daemon used on most Linux distros alongside or instead of systemd's journald. It processes logs using rules (facility.severity → destination) and can forward logs to remote servers. Config files live in /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/.

examples.desc: Send test message and verify delivery
Check where error-level messages are routed
Forward all logs to remote syslog server via TCP

commands.pro_tip: Use `rsyslogd -N1` to validate config before restarting — a syntax error in rsyslog.conf silently stops all logging, which you'll only notice during an incident.

commands.name: logrotate
commands.summary: Automatically rotate, compress, and manage log files.
commands.risk_reason: Misconfigured rotation can delete logs or fill disk.
commands.explanation: logrotate manages log file rotation on a schedule — compressing old logs, deleting logs older than N days, and sending signals to services to reopen log files. Config in /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d/. Run by cron or systemd timer daily.

flags.desc: Dry run — show what would happen without doing it
Force rotation even if not due

examples.desc: Dry run nginx log rotation config

commands.pro_tip: Always test new logrotate configs with `-d` (dry run) first. Common mistake: missing `postrotate` signal to the daemon to reopen files — without it, the service keeps writing to the rotated file.

commands.name: cron
commands.summary: Schedule recurring tasks using the system cron daemon.
commands.risk_reason: Cron jobs run silently; errors can go unnoticed for days.
cautions: Cron runs silently — send output to a log or mail so failures are noticed.
Use full paths and set PATH explicitly in the crontab.
Prevent overlapping runs with `flock -n /tmp/job.lock <command>`.
commands.explanation: Cron runs scheduled commands based on a time expression (minute hour day month weekday). System cron jobs live in /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/, etc. User cron jobs are managed via crontab. Each field: minute(0-59) hour(0-23) day(1-31) month(1-12) weekday(0-7).

examples.desc: List cron jobs for specific user

commands.pro_tip: Always redirect cron output: `command >> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1`. Without redirection, errors go to the user's mail (often ignored). Also set MAILTO='' in crontab to suppress email if not needed.

commands.name: systemd timer
commands.summary: Systemd timer units as a modern alternative to cron.
commands.risk_reason: Timer units require corresponding service units.
commands.explanation: Systemd timers replace cron for scheduled tasks, offering dependency management, precise logging via journald, and missed-run catch-up (Persistent=true). A timer unit (.timer) pairs with a service unit (.service) that defines what to run.

examples.desc: List all timers and their next trigger time
Check status of a specific timer
Enable and start a timer immediately
View logs of the timer's associated service

commands.pro_tip: Use `systemd-analyze calendar 'your-expression'` to validate timer calendar expressions before deploying — shows next 10 trigger times, saving debugging time.

commands.name: nsenter
commands.summary: Enter the namespaces of another process.
commands.risk_reason: Provides access to isolated process namespaces including network and PID.
cautions: Entering a container’s namespaces as root bypasses its isolation; with the mount/PID namespaces your commands can affect the host.
Use it for diagnostics (network namespace) rather than changing state.
commands.explanation: nsenter runs a program in the namespace(s) of an existing process. Essential for debugging containerized processes — enter a container's network namespace to run network tools that aren't available inside the container, or debug a pod's network stack using host tools.

examples.desc: Run ss inside a container's network namespace
Show network interfaces from another process's view

safer.why: Enter only the network namespace (-n) for read-only diagnostics.

commands.pro_tip: Use nsenter to debug distroless or scratch containers that have no shell — run `nsenter -t <container-pid> -n tcpdump` from the host to capture traffic inside a container with no tools.

commands.name: unshare
commands.summary: Run a program with some namespaces unshared from the parent.
commands.risk_reason: Can create isolated environments that are hard to clean up.
cautions: Creates namespaces that persist while any process uses them — hard to clean up if forgotten.
`unshare -r` maps you to root inside a user namespace, which widens the kernel attack surface.
commands.explanation: unshare creates new namespaces (network, PID, mount, user, UTS) and runs a command in them, isolated from the parent. Used to understand container internals, test namespace isolation, and create lightweight sandboxes without full container runtime.

examples.desc: Shell with its own isolated network namespace (no interfaces)
Shell with root privileges in user namespace
Isolated PID namespace (only sees own processes)

commands.pro_tip: Use `unshare --net bash` to test how your app behaves with no network — quickly reveals hardcoded DNS lookups or network dependencies you didn't know existed.

commands.name: cgroups
commands.summary: Inspect and manage control groups that limit process resources.
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect limits can OOM-kill processes or starve services.
cautions: Setting memory/CPU limits too low OOM-kills or throttles services.
Use `systemctl set-property` (or unit drop-ins) rather than writing to /sys/fs/cgroup directly so changes persist.
commands.explanation: Cgroups (control groups) limit and account for CPU, memory, I/O, and network resources used by groups of processes. Containers use cgroups heavily. The systemd-cgls and systemd-cgtop tools visualize the cgroup hierarchy. Direct manipulation is via /sys/fs/cgroup/.

examples.desc: Live resource usage by cgroup (like top for cgroups)
Show cgroups for a specific PID
Set memory limit on a systemd service

commands.pro_tip: Use `systemctl set-property myservice.service CPUQuota=50%` and `MemoryLimit=1G` to apply resource limits to any systemd service without touching container runtimes.

commands.name: chroot
commands.summary: Change the root directory for a process and its children.
commands.risk_reason: Can be used to access filesystems in ways that bypass host permissions.
cautions: A chroot is not a security boundary — root inside it can escape.
Binaries in an incomplete chroot fail with confusing errors; bind-mount /proc, /sys and /dev when repairing systems.
Double-check which directory you chroot into.
commands.explanation: chroot changes the apparent root directory for a process, isolating it from the rest of the filesystem. Used for system rescue (booting into a broken system's filesystem), building packages in clean environments, and as the foundation for containers.

examples.desc: Chroot into a mounted system for rescue
Reset root password on mounted system
Full rescue chroot with devices and proc

safer.why: Verify the mounts of the target tree before chrooting.

commands.pro_tip: For a full rescue chroot, always bind-mount /dev, /proc, /sys, and /run before chrooting — without them, systemd, udev, and many tools will fail with cryptic errors.

commands.name: pgrep
commands.summary: Find process IDs by name or other attributes.
commands.explanation: pgrep finds PIDs matching name patterns or other criteria without parsing ps output. Returns just PIDs, making it ideal for scripting. pkill (its sibling) sends signals to matched processes. The -a flag includes the full command line.

examples.desc: List all Java processes with full command
Find all processes owned by www-data
Match processes by full command line pattern
Send HUP to all nginx workers

commands.pro_tip: Use `pgrep -f 'pattern'` instead of `ps aux | grep | awk` — cleaner, no accidental self-match, and returns just PIDs for direct use in commands.

commands.name: pkill
commands.summary: Send signals to processes matched by name or attributes.
commands.risk_reason: Can kill unintended processes if pattern is too broad.
cautions: Matching is by substring: `pkill java` kills every JVM on the host.
Preview with `pgrep -a <pattern>`; prefer `pkill -x` (exact) or `-u <user>`.
SIGKILL (-9) skips cleanup.
commands.explanation: pkill sends signals to all processes matching a name pattern or other criteria. The default signal is SIGTERM (graceful shutdown). With -9 (SIGKILL), it force-kills. Always verify with pgrep first — pkill applies to all matches.

flags.desc: Send SIGHUP (reload config for many daemons)

examples.desc: Terminate all processes owned by www-data
Kill stale workers by command pattern
Verify then force-kill all Java processes

commands.pro_tip: Always run `pgrep -a pattern` before `pkill pattern` to see exactly what will be affected — pkill's output tells you nothing about what it killed.

commands.name: systemctl advanced
commands.summary: Advanced systemd service management: dependencies, drop-ins, and masking.
commands.risk_reason: Masking and disabling services affects system functionality.
cautions: Masking a unit prevents any start — even by dependencies; remember to unmask.
`isolate`, `rescue` and `emergency` stop most services immediately.
`systemctl edit` creates drop-ins; run daemon-reload and verify with `systemctl cat`.
commands.explanation: Beyond start/stop/status, systemctl manages service dependencies, unit file overrides (drop-ins), masking (preventing any start), and systemd's boot analysis. Drop-in files in /etc/systemd/system/service.d/ override specific unit directives without editing originals.

examples.desc: Show the effective unit file including drop-ins
Create a drop-in override for nginx unit
Permanently prevent postfix from starting (even by dependencies)
Show services ranked by boot time
Show the critical path in boot sequence

commands.pro_tip: Use `systemctl edit service` for drop-in overrides instead of editing unit files directly — overrides survive package upgrades and are clearly separated in `/etc/systemd/system/service.d/override.conf`.

commands.name: htop
commands.risk_reason: Read-only view, but F9/k sends signals to processes.
cautions: Pressing F9/k then Enter sends a signal to the selected process — check the PID highlighted.
Run as a normal user for read-only viewing; only use root when you must signal other users’ processes.
commands.explanation: Colourful top replacement with tree view, search and kill. F5 tree, F6 sort, F9 kill, F4 filter.

commands.name: killall
commands.risk_reason: Signals every process with a matching name — on Solaris-like systems killall kills ALL processes.
cautions: Kills every instance on the host, including processes from other users or containers (if you are root).
`killall` without a name on non-Linux Unixes terminates everything.
Use SIGTERM first; SIGKILL skips cleanup and can corrupt data.
commands.explanation: On Linux killall <name> sends a signal (TERM by default) to every process with that exact name.

examples.desc: Ask before killing each nginx process

commands.name: service
commands.summary: Run a SysV init script / systemctl wrapper
cautions: Restart drops active connections — reload if supported.
Stopping sshd, networking or firewalls on a remote host can lock you out.
commands.explanation: `service name action` is a compatibility wrapper; on systemd it calls systemctl.

commands.name: chkconfig
commands.summary: Manage SysV services at boot (RHEL legacy)
commands.risk_reason: Changes which services start at boot.
cautions: Disabling a critical service (network, sshd) breaks the host at next boot.
commands.explanation: Legacy tool for enabling/disabling init scripts; use systemctl on modern systems.

commands.name: last
cautions: Output contains usernames and source IPs — treat as sensitive.
commands.explanation: Reads /var/log/wtmp to show past logins, reboots and shutdowns.

commands.name: lastb
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; reveals attacker IPs and usernames (sensitive).
cautions: Failed logins may contain passwords mistakenly typed as usernames — protect the output.
commands.explanation: Reads /var/log/btmp. Needs root. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lastb` for the full reference.

commands.name: w
commands.summary: Show who is logged in and what they run
commands.explanation: Displays logged-in users, idle time and their current commands plus load averages.

commands.name: who
commands.explanation: Lists current login sessions. See the flags and examples below, and run `man who` for the full reference.

commands.name: id
commands.explanation: Shows UID, GID and supplementary groups for a user.

commands.name: whoami
commands.explanation: Prints the effective username. See the flags and examples below, and run `man whoami` for the full reference.

commands.name: groups
commands.explanation: Prints the groups of a user. See the flags and examples below, and run `man groups` for the full reference.

commands.name: hostname
commands.risk_reason: Setting the hostname changes system identity.
cautions: Changing it can break monitoring, certificates, clustering and Kubernetes node registration — use hostnamectl and plan the change.
commands.explanation: Without arguments prints the hostname; with an argument sets it until reboot.

commands.name: localectl
cautions: A wrong locale can break scripts that parse tool output; test in a session first.
commands.explanation: Show or set system locale, keyboard layout and X11 keymap via systemd-localed.

commands.name: loginctl
commands.risk_reason: Can terminate sessions and users, including your own.
cautions: terminate-user/terminate-session kills all that user’s processes — including unsaved work and your own SSH session.
enable-linger lets a user keep processes running with no login; review who has it.
commands.explanation: Query and control systemd-logind: list sessions, lock/terminate sessions, enable linger.

flags.desc: End all of a user’s sessions
Let user services run without a login

examples.desc: Keep alice’s services running after logout

safer.why: Check which session is which first

commands.name: reboot
commands.risk_reason: Disconnects all users and stops all services.
cautions: Check who is logged in and what is running (who, systemctl list-jobs) before rebooting.
On remote hosts confirm sshd, networking and fstab are valid or you may lose access.
Schedule maintenance windows and drain nodes (kubectl drain) first.
commands.explanation: Restarts the machine via systemd. May be immediate.

flags.caution: Skips orderly shutdown; can corrupt data.

examples.desc: Reboot in 5 minutes with a message

commands.name: shutdown
commands.summary: Power off or reboot the system
commands.risk_reason: Stops all services and may make remote machines unreachable.
cautions: `shutdown -h now` on a remote host powers it off — you may not be able to turn it back on.
Notify users and drain workloads first.
commands.explanation: Schedules a halt, poweroff or reboot with a warning message.

safer.why: Cancel if it was a mistake

commands.name: poweroff
commands.risk_reason: Shuts the host down; remote machines may not come back.
cautions: Cannot be undone remotely unless the host has out-of-band management.
commands.explanation: Equivalent to shutdown -P now. See the flags and examples below, and run `man poweroff` for the full reference.

commands.name: lsmod
commands.explanation: Shows loaded kernel modules and their usage counts.

examples.desc: Check if a module is loaded

commands.name: modinfo
commands.explanation: Prints details and parameters of a module.

commands.name: modprobe
commands.risk_reason: Loading/unloading modules affects kernel stability and hardware.
cautions: Removing a module in use for network or storage drivers can drop connectivity or disks.
Out-of-tree modules can taint or crash the kernel — test first.
commands.explanation: Adds or removes modules with dependencies resolved. Persistent configuration lives in /etc/modprobe.d/.

commands.name: dmidecode
cautions: Output includes serial numbers/UUIDs — treat as sensitive.
commands.explanation: Prints hardware details including serial numbers and memory slots.

commands.name: lspci
commands.explanation: Shows PCI devices such as NICs and GPUs.

commands.name: lsusb
commands.explanation: Lists USB buses and devices. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lsusb` for the full reference.

commands.name: lshw
commands.explanation: Detailed hardware inventory. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lshw` for the full reference.

commands.name: sensors
commands.explanation: lm-sensors output for CPU, fans and voltages.

commands.name: nice
commands.summary: Run a command with a lower priority
cautions: Negative values need root and can starve other processes.
commands.explanation: Adjusts niceness (−20 high priority to 19 low).

examples.desc: Run a backup at low priority

commands.name: renice
commands.summary: Change priority of a running process
commands.risk_reason: Raising priority can starve other workloads.
cautions: Negative niceness on busy hosts can make the system unresponsive.
commands.explanation: Changes the niceness of running processes.

commands.name: ionice
cautions: Realtime class (1) can starve other processes of disk access.
commands.explanation: Control disk I/O priority of a process. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ionice` for the full reference.

examples.desc: Run copy at idle I/O priority

commands.name: pstree
commands.explanation: Visualises parent/child relationships. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pstree` for the full reference.

commands.name: pidof
commands.explanation: Prints PIDs for a program name. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pidof` for the full reference.

commands.name: mpstat
commands.explanation: sysstat tool showing per-core utilisation.

commands.name: pidstat
commands.explanation: sysstat tool reporting CPU, memory and I/O per process.

commands.name: ldd
commands.risk_reason: Some ldd implementations execute the target binary.
cautions: Never run ldd on untrusted binaries — use `objdump -p file | grep NEEDED` or `readelf -d` instead.
commands.explanation: Shows which shared libraries a binary needs. glibc ldd may run the program.

commands.name: getcap
commands.explanation: Lists Linux capabilities set on files. See the flags and examples below, and run `man getcap` for the full reference.

commands.name: setcap
commands.risk_reason: Grants privileged powers to a binary; misuse creates privilege-escalation paths.
cautions: Capabilities like cap_sys_admin or cap_setuid are effectively root.
They are lost when the file is replaced by an upgrade.
commands.explanation: Assigns capabilities such as cap_net_bind_service to executables.

commands.name: auditctl
commands.risk_reason: Wrong rules can flood logs or, with -e 2, lock the audit configuration until reboot.
cautions: Rules that match busy paths can generate gigabytes of logs and fill /var.
-e 2 makes rules immutable until reboot.
-D removes all rules including compliance ones.
commands.explanation: Add, list and delete kernel audit rules.

commands.name: ausearch
commands.explanation: Query auditd logs by key, type or time. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ausearch` for the full reference.

commands.name: systemctl stop
commands.risk_reason: Stops the service immediately; dependants may fail; stopping sshd/network can lock you out.
cautions: Check what depends on the unit and whether you reach the host through it (sshd, NetworkManager, firewalld).
Production stops cause outages — drain from the load balancer first.
commands.explanation: Stops a unit. Unlike restart, nothing brings it back.

commands.name: systemctl restart
commands.risk_reason: Drops connections and briefly interrupts the service.
cautions: Validate the configuration first (nginx -t, sshd -t, apachectl configtest).
Restart of databases and message brokers can take minutes and trigger failovers.
commands.explanation: Stops then starts a unit; use reload for configuration changes where supported.

commands.name: systemctl disable
commands.risk_reason: The service will not start after the next reboot.
cautions: Disabling network, ssh or firewall units can make the next reboot unreachable.
commands.explanation: Removes the enable symlinks. --now also stops it immediately.

commands.name: systemctl mask
commands.summary: Make a unit impossible to start
commands.risk_reason: Even dependencies and manual starts fail until unmasked.
cautions: Masked units cause confusing “Unit is masked” failures later — document them.
commands.explanation: Links the unit to /dev/null. See the flags and examples below, and run `man systemctl` for the full reference.

commands.name: systemctl daemon-reload
commands.risk_reason: Re-reads all unit files; does not restart services.
cautions: Services keep running with the old definition until restarted.
commands.explanation: Needed after editing unit files or drop-ins.

commands.name: systemctl edit
cautions: Keep overrides in Git/config management.
commands.explanation: Creates /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/override.conf.

commands.name: journalctl -u
commands.explanation: Shows journal entries for a systemd unit.

commands.name: anacron
commands.summary: Cron for machines not always on
commands.explanation: Ensures daily/weekly jobs run after downtime.

commands.name: flock
commands.explanation: Wraps a command with a file lock. See the flags and examples below, and run `man flock` for the full reference.

commands.name: lsns
commands.explanation: Shows Linux namespaces in use. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lsns` for the full reference.

commands.name: sudoedit
cautions: Validate config syntax before reloading the service.
commands.explanation: Opens a temporary copy in your editor and writes it back as root.

commands.name: script
commands.risk_reason: Logs everything you type and see (including passwords).
cautions: The log can contain passwords and secrets — protect it.
commands.explanation: Saves a transcript. See the flags and examples below, and run `man script` for the full reference.

commands.name: reset
commands.explanation: Fixes a garbled terminal. See the flags and examples below, and run `man reset` for the full reference.

commands.name: lastlog
commands.explanation: Reads /var/log/lastlog. See the flags and examples below, and run `man lastlog` for the full reference.

commands.name: getconf
commands.explanation: Prints system configuration values. See the flags and examples below, and run `man getconf` for the full reference.

commands.name: numactl
commands.explanation: Run processes with NUMA policies. See the flags and examples below, and run `man numactl` for the full reference.
cautions: Binding memory to one NUMA node can cause out-of-memory errors even when other nodes have free memory.
Test policy changes on staging; wrong CPU/memory binding degrades latency-sensitive services.

commands.name: taskset
cautions: Mis-pinning degrades latency.
commands.explanation: Bind processes to CPUs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man taskset` for the full reference.

commands.name: chrt
commands.risk_reason: Real-time priority can starve the system.
cautions: SCHED_FIFO/RR processes that loop will freeze other tasks.
commands.explanation: Sets scheduling policy/priority. See the flags and examples below, and run `man chrt` for the full reference.

commands.name: hwclock
commands.risk_reason: Setting the clock causes time jumps.
cautions: Time jumps break TLS, Kerberos, replication and logs.
commands.explanation: Shows or sets the RTC. See the flags and examples below, and run `man hwclock` for the full reference.

commands.name: ntpdate
commands.summary: Set the clock once from an NTP server
cautions: Stepping time can break running services; use chrony/systemd-timesyncd.
commands.explanation: Legacy one-shot time sync. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ntpdate` for the full reference.

commands.name: busctl
cautions: `call` can trigger privileged actions.
commands.explanation: Inspect and call D-Bus services. See the flags and examples below, and run `man busctl` for the full reference.

commands.name: systemd-cat
commands.explanation: Pipe a command output into journald. See the flags and examples below, and run `man systemd-cat` for the full reference.
